analysis.one_liner: Strips the EPA's power to set carbon limits on coal- and gas-fired power plants.
analysis.headline: A Senate committee sent the bill to the floor in October 2015 with 36 sponsors behind it, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop the EPA from carrying out its rules limiting carbon pollution from power plants. It would wipe out the rules already issued, set conditions that would make any future carbon standard nearly impossible to write, and let a state's governor unilaterally declare the state exempt from compliance. It would also push compliance deadlines back until every court challenge was fully finished.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mining companies and utilities that burn coal would keep running without any federal carbon limit, and existing rules targeting their emissions would be erased. Governors would gain a new power to pull their states out of compliance with a written notice, and natural gas plant operators would also gain from lighter treatment. The bill's sponsors framed the ratepayer opt-out and compliance delay as protection for electricity customers, who might otherwise face higher bills during a transition away from coal.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares a series of existing EPA proposed rules on power plant carbon emissions to have never been issued, erasing them retroactively.

It forbids the EPA from setting a carbon standard for new coal plants unless that standard has already been achieved for a full year at six operating plants on a commercial basis, and bars the agency from counting government-funded demonstration projects; because the standard in question rests on carbon capture technology that is not running at commercial plants, this condition would likely make any standard impossible to issue.

It lets a state governor, by notifying the EPA, exempt the state from any plan to cut power plant carbon if the governor decides it would hurt jobs, grid reliability, or electricity rates — including for low-income ratepayers.

It pushes back every compliance deadline for the existing-plant rule until all court challenges to it are completely finished, and removes any penalty — such as a highway funding sanction — for states that do not comply.

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, the cost falls on people exposed to power plant pollution and on anyone affected by climate change, since federal carbon limits for the country's largest single source of that pollution would be erased or made unenforceable. Supporters would counter that electricity customers, especially in coal states, would have paid higher rates under the rules being nullified.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near power plants and the climate

drawbacks.text: Nullifying the power plant carbon rules would leave the largest American source of carbon dioxide unregulated under the provision of the Clean Air Act at issue, with no substitute federal limit.
The governor opt-out means any single state executive, without a vote of its legislature, could decline to cut power plant emissions at all, gutting the rule nationwide if enough states did so.

The requirement that a standard be proven for a year at six operating plants, with demonstration projects excluded, is a hurdle the underlying technology could not clear in commercial operation, so the bill functions as a near-permanent prohibition rather than a delay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow almost entirely to coal producers and coal-burning utilities, while its costs — continued carbon and other air pollution from plants that would otherwise face limits — fall broadly on the public. Its ratepayer-protection framing addresses a real concern about electricity prices, but the governor opt-out and the effectively unreachable technology standard go far beyond shielding customers from rate spikes; they would prevent any federal carbon limit for power plants from functioning.

outcome.mechanism: The Environment and Public Works Committee approved it and placed it on the Senate's calendar, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 13, 2015, by Senator Capito of West Virginia with 35 cosponsors, 34 of them Republicans and one, Senator Manchin of West Virginia, a Democrat.

A Senate subcommittee held a hearing in June 2015, and the Environment and Public Works Committee ordered the bill reported favorably in August and formally reported it without amendment on October 29, 2015, with committee Democrats filing minority views.

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, where a bill waits for leadership to schedule floor time; no such time was ever scheduled, and the bill received no floor vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the EPA's power plant carbon rules were never erased or made unenforceable by Congress. The public kept the prospect of federal carbon limits, while coal interests gained nothing beyond what litigation outside Congress already gave them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept the rules on the books

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Republican — 34 of the 35 cosponsors — with coal-state Democrat Joe Manchin the lone exception, and committee Democrats formally opposed the bill in their minority views.

industries.note: The bill would erase the federal carbon rules that threaten demand for coal-fired electricity, protecting coal's market. That protection comes at the cost of the pollution those rules were written to limit.

Utilities running existing coal plants would face no federal carbon limit, no state plan obligations they could not avoid through a governor's notice, and compliance deadlines postponed until all litigation ends. The public bears the emissions those plants would continue to release.

The bill requires the EPA to treat gas plants as a separate category from coal and nullifies the proposed rules covering new plants of both kinds, easing the regulatory outlook for new gas construction. Its interest in weaker carbon rules still runs against climate protection.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and carbon capture developers
industries.note: By nullifying the rules that drive utilities toward cleaner generation and barring demonstration-project results from any future standard, the bill would remove demand that solar, wind, and carbon capture projects depend on. Their loss tracks the public's loss of emission reductions.
